title: People watch Project Dawn and ask the same question!
author: avaSupernova
selftext:
That's the question I get most on our Project Dawn streams, so it's worth answering properly — because the assumption behind it is wrong in an interesting way.



Short version: no. I build the game. But the AI is doing something real, and it isn't the thing people think.



Some context. Project Dawn is a game I'm building in Unreal 5.7 — unedited, live, on stream. I'm not an Unreal expert. I'm a person who wanted to build a game and found that the parts I didn't know were the wall I kept hitting: the rigging, the animation blends, how you actually get a weapon into a character's hand so it doesn't look like it's floating.



On stream, when I hit one of those, I ask. There's an assistant I've built — Ava — that knows the engine, knows the project, and remembers what we did last session. It tells me what I'm looking at and what the next step is. Then I go and do it. Often I do it badly, then fix it. Nothing here is automated; if it were, there'd be nothing to watch.



So the honest framing isn't "AI builds a game." It's closer to "someone who couldn't have done this alone can now do it with a guide." Those are very different claims, and only the second one is true.



Why I think that matters beyond my own project: the thing that stops people building is usually not talent, it's a specific gap — one part of the toolchain you don't know and can't afford to spend months learning. If something can hold that gap open while you carry on, that's a real change in who gets to make things. Not because the machine made the decision for you, but because you didn't have to know everything before you were allowed to start.



Full disclosure, since this is essentially a post about a tool I make: yes, I build the assistant, and yes, it's open source (Apache 2.0, runs with your own API key). But the point of the post isn't the tool. It's that the "AI does it all" framing is worse than the truth in both directions — it overstates what the machine does, and it undersells what becomes possible for the person driving it.



You don't need all the answers. You need to know what you want.



I'm figuring this out in public anyway, so engine and rigging questions are welcome in the comments.
